subject: business-studies
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Taylor's theory of scientific management assumes that workers are primarily motivated by:
options: Self-actualisation
Money and economic reward
Recognition and responsibility
Social belonging and team relationships
questions.explain: Taylor argued workers are 'economic men' motivated chiefly by pay, leading to piece-rate systems.

questions.q: In Maslow's hierarchy of needs, which level must generally be satisfied before esteem needs?
options: Aesthetic needs
Self-actualisation
Social (love/belonging) needs
Self-fulfilment
questions.explain: Maslow's order is physiological, safety, social, esteem, then self-actualisation, so social needs precede esteem.

questions.q: Induction training is best defined as training that:
options: Develops senior managers for promotion
Introduces a new employee to the organisation and their role
Teaches specialist craft skills over several years
Is delivered away from the workplace by experts
questions.explain: Induction training familiarises new starters with the firm, their job and procedures.

questions.q: Labour productivity is best calculated as:
options: Total output divided by the number of employees
Total revenue divided by total costs
Total output multiplied by number of employees
Number of employees divided by total output
questions.explain: Labour productivity measures output per worker, found by dividing total output by the number of employees.

questions.q: Hard HRM treats employees primarily as:
options: A resource/cost to be used efficiently and flexibly
Members of a single family unit
Equal partners in strategic decisions
A valued asset to be developed and empowered
questions.explain: Hard HRM views workers as a resource to be deployed cost-effectively, in contrast to soft HRM.

questions.q: Job enrichment involves:
options: Giving workers more challenging tasks and greater responsibility
Giving workers more tasks at the same level of difficulty
Cutting the number of tasks each worker performs
Rotating workers between simple repetitive jobs
questions.explain: Job enrichment adds more demanding tasks and responsibility (vertical loading) to make work more fulfilling.

questions.q: A laissez-faire leadership style is most likely to be effective when:
options: A crisis requires fast top-down decisions
Staff are highly skilled, motivated and self-directing
Tasks are highly routine and standardised
Staff are inexperienced and need close direction
questions.explain: Laissez-faire leaves staff to work autonomously, which suits skilled, self-motivated professionals.

questions.q: An autocratic leadership style is characterised by:
options: Decisions delegated entirely to employees
Decisions reached by group consensus
Decisions made by the leader with little consultation
No decisions being made at all
questions.explain: Autocratic leaders make decisions themselves and expect compliance, with little staff input.

questions.q: Which best describes the trend of delegation in a business?
options: Removing layers of management
Passing authority for a task down the hierarchy to a subordinate
Centralising all decisions at head office
Combining functions into project teams
questions.explain: Delegation passes authority (not ultimate responsibility) for tasks down to subordinates.

questions.q: A high rate of labour retention is most likely to:
options: Always reduce labour productivity
Signal that wages are too high
Increase recruitment and training costs
Reduce costs and preserve organisational knowledge
questions.explain: Retaining staff lowers recruitment/training costs and keeps experienced workers' knowledge within the firm.

questions.q: A matrix organisational structure is best described as one where employees:
options: Are grouped strictly by geographic region
Work across functions, reporting to both a functional and a project manager
Report only to a single line manager
Have no formal hierarchy at all
questions.explain: In a matrix structure staff belong to a function but also work on projects, answering to two managers.

questions.q: The Hawthorne effect, identified by Elton Mayo, suggests that productivity rises when:
options: Pay is linked directly to output
Managers adopt a strictly autocratic style
Workers feel they are receiving attention and are valued
Tasks are broken into the smallest possible parts
questions.explain: Mayo found output improved because workers felt observed and valued, highlighting social/human factors.

questions.q: On the Tannenbaum-Schmidt continuum, moving from left to right shows:
options: Decreasing manager authority and increasing subordinate freedom
A shift from democratic to autocratic styles only
No change in the balance of authority
Increasing manager authority and decreasing subordinate freedom
questions.explain: The continuum runs from manager-led (boss-centred) to subordinate-led (freedom for staff) leadership.

questions.q: A democratic leadership style typically involves:
options: The leader consulting employees before making decisions
Leaving all decisions to individual workers
The leader imposing decisions without discussion
Avoiding decision-making responsibility
questions.explain: Democratic leaders consult and involve employees in decisions while retaining final responsibility.

questions.q: Centralisation of decision-making is most likely to be an advantage when a business needs:
options: Consistency and tight control across the organisation
To develop junior managers' decision skills
To reduce the workload of senior managers
Rapid local responses to varied markets
questions.explain: Centralisation gives senior managers tight, consistent control over decisions across the firm.

questions.q: Empowerment as a motivational method primarily aims to:
options: Replace all financial rewards
Increase managerial control over employees
Reduce the variety of tasks workers do
Give employees more authority to make their own decisions
questions.explain: Empowerment delegates authority to employees, increasing their autonomy and engagement.

questions.q: Internal recruitment, compared with external recruitment, usually:
options: Always requires a longer induction period
Is cheaper and quicker and boosts staff morale
Widens the pool of available candidates
Brings in completely new ideas and skills
questions.explain: Recruiting from within is cheaper, faster and motivating, though it can limit fresh ideas.

questions.q: Which of the following is a Herzberg motivator rather than a hygiene factor?
options: Achievement and recognition
Salary
Working conditions
Company policy
questions.explain: Motivators such as achievement, recognition and responsibility drive satisfaction; the others are hygiene factors.

questions.q: Which formula correctly gives the absenteeism rate?
options: (Number of staff days absent ÷ total possible working days) × 100
(Total wages ÷ number of staff) × 100
(Number of staff who left ÷ total staff) × 100
Output ÷ number of staff present
questions.explain: Absenteeism rate = (number of staff days lost to absence ÷ total possible working days) × 100.

questions.q: In Herzberg's two-factor theory, hygiene factors are best described as factors that:
options: Always include responsibility and achievement
Are the same as motivators
Directly motivate workers to perform better
Prevent dissatisfaction but do not themselves motivate
questions.explain: Herzberg's hygiene factors (e.g. pay, conditions) prevent dissatisfaction but do not actively motivate.

questions.q: The span of control refers to:
options: The number of subordinates directly answerable to a manager
The chain of command from top to bottom
The degree of decision-making authority delegated
The number of layers in the hierarchy
questions.explain: Span of control is the number of subordinates directly accountable to one manager.

questions.q: Setting a specific HR objective, such as reducing labour turnover to 10%, is most useful because it:
options: Removes the need to measure performance
Provides a measurable target to plan towards and assess
Replaces the need for any motivation strategy
Guarantees the objective will be met
questions.explain: A specific, measurable HR objective allows the firm to plan, monitor and evaluate performance.

questions.q: Which is an example of a non-financial method of motivation?
options: Commission
Teamworking
Performance-related pay
Profit sharing
questions.explain: Teamworking is a non-financial method; the others are financial reward systems.

questions.q: Collective bargaining is the process by which:
options: Shareholders decide directors' pay
Trade unions negotiate pay and conditions on behalf of members
Each employee negotiates pay individually with the employer
Government sets wage rates for all firms
questions.explain: Collective bargaining is negotiation of terms between employers and unions representing groups of workers.

questions.q: A piece-rate payment system pays workers according to:
options: A fixed annual salary
The number of hours worked
Company profits shared equally
The number of units they produce
questions.explain: Piece rate links pay directly to output, paying a set amount per unit produced.

questions.q: Off-the-job training refers to training that takes place:
options: Exclusively through job rotation
Away from the immediate work area, e.g. on a course
Only after the employee has resigned
At the employee's normal workstation while working
questions.explain: Off-the-job training occurs away from the workplace, such as at college or on external courses.

questions.q: Which is a key benefit of decentralisation?
options: Senior managers retain tight control over all decisions
Local managers can respond quickly to local conditions
It reduces the need to train junior staff
Decisions are made more consistently across the whole firm
questions.explain: Decentralisation pushes authority down so local managers can make faster, more responsive decisions.

questions.q: Delayering an organisation typically results in:
options: Greater centralisation of decisions
More layers of middle management
A taller hierarchy with narrower spans of control
A flatter hierarchy with wider spans of control
questions.explain: Removing layers of management flattens the structure and widens each remaining manager's span of control.

questions.q: A firm has 200 staff; 30 leave and are replaced during the year. Its labour turnover is:
questions.explain: Labour turnover = (staff leaving ÷ average number employed) × 100 = (30 ÷ 200) × 100 = 15%.

questions.q: A key potential benefit to a business of recognising a trade union is:
options: Complete control over employee pay
The elimination of all industrial action
Guaranteed lower wage costs every year
Negotiating with one body rather than many individuals
questions.explain: A recognised union lets the firm bargain collectively with one representative body, simplifying negotiations.
